Orchot Tzadikim 26:97: And if the sinner who comes to do teshuvah is a person who cannot study, or is burdened [with family responsibilities], or is an ignorant person, or is learned but cannot force himself to keep all the words of this book — for all these one should be strict in having them bear harsh suffering. But suffering is not the same for every person, for there is a person who is very healthy, and one who is weak. Behold, when the court sat in Jerusalem in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, judging capital cases and cases of flogging, they would assess the flogging according to the strength of the man being flogged. And so one must do now, all according to the person's own condition: there is a person who, if dealt with too strictly regarding suffering, will abandon it entirely and not do teshuvah at all. Therefore the wise man must investigate the person's situation, and instruct according to what he sees fit.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:98: And now I must write the matters of suffering appropriate to each transgression. One who had relations with a gentile woman should fast and be flogged, and should not eat meat or drink wine for at least forty days; or should fast three days and nights, three times, once a year, for three years. And if after teshuvah he returns to his former ways, be stricter with him: in the summer he should go to a place with many ants and sit among them naked, and in the winter he should break the ice and sit in the water up to his nose. And if he returns again to his former ways, be stricter still.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:99: One who emits seed in vain should fast forty days, even if not consecutive. And he should sit in water in winter for the time it takes to roast and swallow an egg, throughout all forty days; and he should not eat meat or drink wine or anything hot, except on Sabbaths and festivals. And he should wash his head a little with water two or three times, throughout all those forty days.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:100: If he embraced or kissed his wife while she was menstrually impure, he should fast forty days. One who had relations with his wife while menstrually impure should fast forty consecutive days and be flogged every day; and he should not eat meat or drink wine or eat hot food, except on Sabbaths and festivals. And he should not bathe throughout all those days, and should confess every day. One who kisses or embraces other women should fast Monday and Thursday, and keep far from the entrance to her house. One who had relations with an animal, wild beast, or bird should fast and not bathe for forty days, and should not look at animals, beasts, and birds while they mate with one another.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:101: A murderer should go into exile for three years, and be flogged in every single city and say, "I am a murderer." And he should not eat meat or drink wine, and should not shave the hair of his head and beard except once a month. And he should bind the hand with which he murdered, and his arm, with iron, and around his neck, and go barefoot, and weep over his sin, and fast every day until he completes his fasting and his exile. And afterward he should fast for one year, Monday, Thursday, and Monday. If people revile him, he should be silent. And during those three years he should not go on outings or engage in merriment. And when he is exiled, he should lie down before the entrance of the synagogue, and let passersby step over him, but not tread upon him.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:102: An apostate should remove his fine garments, and mourn and weep and grieve all the days of his life, and lower his spirit and his pride, and confess three times each day. And he should not eat meat or drink wine except on Sabbaths and festivals. And he should bathe little, and should not wash his head except once or twice a month. And he should not attend merrymaking or weddings, except for the wedding blessing alone. And he should keep far from idolatry and its worshippers, and not sit near priests and monks, nor in a place where words of heresy are spoken; and he should keep far from the entrance of their homes and not benefit from them. And as soon as he returns, he requires immersion. And he should bear suffering and affliction corresponding to his sins: for he denied the fundamental principle, desecrated Sabbaths, had relations with gentile women, and transgressed matters liable for excision and death by the court. Therefore he requires great suffering and great teshuvah.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:103: Whoever has relations with a married woman or a betrothed young woman thereby forbids her to her husband once she is willing, and is liable for death by the court. Therefore he should bear suffering as harsh as death: in the winter he should sit in snow or ice one hour every day, doing this throughout the winter, once, twice, or three times. And in the summer he should sit before flies or bees, or other sufferings as harsh as death, and confess throughout all this with weeping and sighing. And for a full year he should not eat meat or drink wine, except on Sabbaths, festivals, and Purim. And he should not eat hot food, and should bathe only a little on the eves of Sabbaths and festivals. And he should not watch any merrymaking, only listen to the wedding blessing. And he should not indulge himself in anything. And he should be flogged every day, and lie on the ground or on a bare board without pillow or bolster, except on Sabbaths and festivals when he may lie on straw and stubble with a pillow under his head, until he removes the coarse spirit within him and kills his desire. And he should live a life of suffering, and wear sackcloth on his flesh. And he should not speak of the desire for women, and should not gaze at women and their ornaments even when not worn, and should not listen to the sound of their singing. And he should not be with women at all, neither by hint nor in any way; and even with his own wife when she is menstrually impure, he should not seclude himself with her in any way.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:104: One who swears falsely or trespasses against a sacred ban should be flogged several times all the days of his life, and confess for many days. And afterward he should be careful never to swear, even truthfully, neither by the Torah nor by the souls of his ancestors, but should vow by his own life. But he should swear to fulfill the commandments. And he should be careful not to utter the Name of Heaven in vain, and his limbs should tremble when he mentions the Blessed Name. And he should be careful about a blessing in vain; and if he erred and recited a blessing in vain, he should say afterward: "blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" (Yerushalmi Berachot 6:1). And those who accustom their mouths and the mouths of their children to mention the Name of Heaven in bathhouses and in places of filth, and to mention the Name of Heaven in vain — woe to their souls and their children's souls, for they have thus taught their tongue. Therefore let him guard and fence himself and his children and his companions who heed him, from mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain. And if this repentant person was required to take an oath for his creditor, even truthfully, he should fast that same day every year.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:105: If he was accustomed to talking in the synagogue, and to laughter and levity, from the time he returns he should be careful not to speak any mundane matter in the synagogue, even not during the time of prayer. And he should sit in great awe and pray with submission. And he should fast forty days, whether consecutive or spread out, and be flogged privately every day.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:106: Whoever stole or took interest should make restitution, and ask forgiveness for it. And he should fast forty days or more, and confess every day. And he should be careful not to accept deposits, and should not accustom himself to going near his fellow's money. And he should do acts of kindness with his body and his money, and be generous from his own wealth to those who toil in Torah and fear Heaven. And this one who took interest — if he could manage not to take interest even from a gentile, it would be good.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:107: Whoever informs against his fellow makes him hated in the eyes of the ruler, and slanders him, and takes his money, and puts his fellow to death, along with his wife and children who depend on him — he should repay his fellow for all he caused him to lose and ask his forgiveness. And he should be flogged and fast more than two years, and confess all the days of his life, for he is considered as though he had killed his fellow and his wife and children, and however many transgressions he has committed — therefore let him break his spirit. And if he has nothing to pay, let him gather many friends and ask his forgiveness, and pay him back gradually, to him or to his heirs.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:108: A talebearer is likewise, and there is no remedy for him unless he seeks his forgiveness. And he should fast forty days or more, and be flogged every day, and confess all the days of his life. And let all his occupations be with the commandments, and with the pursuit of peace between every person, and between a man and his wife.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:109: Whoever strikes his fellow and causes him grief, whether through money or through wronging him with words, has no atonement unless he pacifies his fellow. And Yom Kippur atones only for transgressions between him and the Omnipresent, but those between him and his fellow require appeasing him (Yoma 85b). Whoever raises his hand against his fellow is called "wicked" (Sanhedrin 58b) — let him seek his forgiveness and be atoned.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:110: Whoever whitens his fellow's face [shames him] should fast forty days or more, and be flogged every day, and confess all the days of his life. Whoever gives his fellow a nickname should seek his forgiveness publicly, and fast forty days, and confess privately every day.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:111: Whoever wrongs a convert should seek his forgiveness, and be flogged, and confess, and fast forty days.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:112: Whoever provokes his fellow should bring three rows of people, and say: "I have sinned, and perverted what was right, and it did not profit me" (based on Job 33:27). And he should ask him three times and no more. And if the person has died, he should bring ten people to his grave, and say: "I have sinned against the Lord, God of Israel, and against this so-and-so, whom I provoked" (Yoma 87a).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:113: And first the provoker should go to the one he provoked, and say: "I have wronged you." And if he does not accept it, he should bring ten people, and ask his forgiveness before them. And this applies specifically if he did not shame him in public; but if he shamed him in public, mere private appeasement is not enough forgiveness. And the one forgiving should not be cruel (Bava Kamma 92a). And if he provoked him and gave him a bad name, there is no forgiveness for him ever (Yerushalmi Bava Kamma 8:7), unless he fasts and is flogged privately for forty days or more.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:114: Whoever desecrates the Name — desecration of the Name is a very great iniquity. And what is desecration of the Name? Rav said (Yoma 86a): such as I, who go to the butcher's shop, and take meat, and do not pay the money at once. Meaning: he brings upon himself the appearance of robbery, and people learn from him and are lax even more. Rabbi Yochanan said: such as I, who walk four cubits without Torah study or tefillin — meaning: people are lax and learn from him to be even more lenient. The school of Rabbi Ami said: whoever's colleagues are ashamed because of reports about him — meaning: they speak of his improper deeds, and people learn from his deeds, and reason a fortiori from him, ruling leniently on actual transgressions. Rabbi Abahu said in the name of Rabbi Chanina (Kiddushin 40a): it is better for a person to commit a transgression in private than to desecrate the Name of Heaven in public — meaning: so that people not learn from his deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:115: And Rabbi Ilai the Elder said: if a person sees his inclination overpowering him, let him go to a place where he is not known, and dress in black and wrap himself in black, and do what his heart desires, rather than desecrate the Name of Heaven in public. And Rabbeinu Chananel explained: heaven forbid that it be permitted for him to commit a transgression; rather, the Sages stood against the evil inclination, which desires only the forbidden and the fulfillment of its craving, and since he goes far away and wears black, his heart will break and he will refrain from the sin. But to actually commit forbidden acts — absolutely not. Rather, these acts break the evil of the inclination, and prevent him from transgressing, as Rabbi Ilai said, for the fatigue of travel and lodging away from home, and wearing black, break the evil inclination and prevent it from transgressions. And they said: whoever does not care for the honor of his Maker deserves not to have come into the world (Chagigah 11b). And they said in the Talmud: Rav Yosef said: this refers to one who commits a transgression in private. And Rabbi Yitzchak said: whoever commits a transgression in private is as though he pushes away the feet of the Divine Presence.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:116: Desecration of the Name is a transgression that bears fruit. For when he does something bad, others learn from him. And of this transgression every person must fear very, very much, for desecration of the Name occurs in many ways and has no measure, for whoever demeans a single commandment and is lax regarding the honor of Heaven is called "one who desecrates the Name," for others will learn from him and be more lax still. Therefore a person must be very, very careful in all his deeds, so that others not learn from him to be lax and lenient.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:117: If a person transgressed matters liable for excision and death by the court, teshuvah and Yom Kippur atone for half, and sufferings atone for half. But if the Name of Heaven was desecrated through him — teshuvah has no power to suspend it, nor does Yom Kippur atone, nor do sufferings cleanse; rather, all of these suspend it, and death cleanses it (Yoma 86a). Therefore let every person be very careful of desecration of the Name, and keep far from the disgraceful and from anything resembling it (Chullin 44b). And the essence of teshuvah for desecration of the Name is that he confess his sins before the multitude, and say to them: "do not learn from me, for I have sinned, committed iniquity, and transgressed, and desecrated the Blessed Name through my folly." And he should fast several fasts, and confess every day until the day of his death.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:118: For every single transgression a person commits, whether unintentionally or deliberately, such as touching a lamp or lighting it without remembering it is the Sabbath, or doing something without knowing — he must confess and fast at least two days: Monday and Thursday. And so for all transgressions, great and small, that a person commits, he should fast. And there are two benefits in this: the first, that the fast atones. The second, that he will refrain from transgressions, for he will think: "if I do this, I will need to fast," and through this he will refrain from the transgression. And this is the great fence against all transgressions — that he impose a penalty on himself: either to give charity or to inflict suffering on his body when he transgresses. And he should do this for all the transgressions he is accustomed to, such as hatred and envy, rejoicing at his fellow's misfortune, idle talk, and slander; or not having intended properly during blessings and prayer, casting off the blessings from his mouth without intent of heart, and all such things. He should examine himself very much every day regarding these matters; if he encountered one of these and transgressed it, he should hasten to grieve and mourn and confess for whatever iniquity he committed, and seek forgiveness from the Blessed Lord with a broken heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:119: Confession is a great matter. For our Sages of blessed memory taught (Sanhedrin 43b): when he was about ten cubits from the place of stoning, they would say to him, "confess!" for such is the way of those about to be executed — they confess, for whoever confesses has a share in the World to Come. So we find with Achan, to whom Joshua said: "my son, give glory to the Lord, God of Israel, and give Him thanks, and tell me now what you have done — do not hide it from me. And Achan answered Joshua and said: truly I have sinned against the Lord, God of Israel, and thus and thus have I done" (Joshua 7:19-20). And from where do we know that confession atoned for him? For it is written, "and Joshua said, why have you troubled us? The Lord shall trouble you this day" (ibid. verse 25) — "this day" you are troubled, but you are not troubled in the World to Come. And if he does not know how to confess, they say to him: say, "let my death be an atonement for all my iniquities."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:120: For all the commandments in the Torah, whether positive or negative, if a person transgressed one of them, whether deliberately or unintentionally, when he does teshuvah and returns from his sin, he is obligated to confess before the Blessed God, as it is said: "a man or woman who commits any of the sins of man, to commit a trespass against the Lord, and that soul is guilty; and they shall confess their sin which they have done" — this is verbal confession. And all who bear sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, and all who are liable for death by the court or flogging — atonement does not come to them through death, or flogging, or a sacrifice, until they do teshuvah and confess. And likewise one who wounds his fellow or damages his fellow's property — even though he has paid him, he is not atoned for until he confesses and returns from ever doing such a thing again. And how does one confess? He says: "please, O Lord! I have sinned, committed iniquity, and transgressed before You, and have done such-and-such. And behold, I regret it and am ashamed of my deeds, and I will never return to this matter again." This is the essence of confession, and whoever confesses at length, elaborating on this matter, is praiseworthy. And this too is the essence of confession: "but we have sinned."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:121: And it is very good to spell out one's own sin within the confession. For instance, if he ate carrion or non-kosher meat, or some other forbidden thing, when he says "I have incurred guilt," he should say, "I have eaten a forbidden thing." And if he sinned through lewdness, when he says "I have betrayed," he should say, "I have had relations of lewdness," and specify whether he had relations with a gentile woman or a menstruating woman. And if he stole, when he says "I have robbed," he should say, "I have stolen and robbed from so-and-so and so-and-so." And if he gave his fellow a bad name, or slandered him, or placed him under any ban, he should say of this, "I have spoken slanderously." And if he emitted seed in vain, when he reaches "I have committed iniquity," he should say, "I have emitted seed in vain." And if he committed lewdness with forbidden relations, when he reaches "I have acted presumptuously," he should say, "I have committed lewdness." And if he desecrated Sabbaths, when he reaches "I have coveted," he should say, "I have desecrated Sabbaths"; and if he coveted, he should say, "I have coveted." And so for the whole alphabet, for each and every letter of the confession, he should say something akin to the transgression he committed. And he should say with weeping: "let the wicked forsake his way, and the man of iniquity his thoughts; and let him return to the Lord, and He will have compassion on him, and to our God, for He will abundantly pardon" (Isaiah 55:7); and then it will benefit him.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:122: And at the end of the confession: "I have turned aside from Your good commandments and judgments, and it has not profited me. And You are righteous concerning all that has come upon me, for You have acted truly, and I have acted wickedly." And then he should say thus: "I have transgressed positive commandments and negative commandments; I have transgressed matters liable for excision and death by the court; I have transgressed the Written Torah, I have transgressed the Oral Torah; I have forgotten Your great Name, I have forgotten the yoke of Your kingship and Your fear; and You are righteous concerning all that has come upon us." And it is found in the Yerushalmi (Yerushalmi Yoma 8:7): how does one confess? "Master of the universe! I have done what is evil in Your eyes, and I have stood in a bad way, and I have walked in the wantonness of my heart, and I have not heeded Your rebukes. And I will no longer do so. May it be Your will, O Lord my God and God of my fathers, that You atone for me for all my transgressions, and forgive me for all my iniquities, and pardon me for all my sins."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:123: In sum: a person should return from all the bad traits. And the bad traits require very great and strong strengthening, for a person is already accustomed to them and finds it hard to separate from them. Of this it is said, "let the wicked forsake his way, and the man of iniquity his thoughts" (Isaiah 55:7). And let not the repentant sinner think he is far removed from the virtues of teshuvah because of the sins and iniquities he has committed — this is not so; rather, he is beloved and cherished before the Blessed Creator, as though he had never sinned at all. And not only that, but his reward is great, for he has tasted the taste of sin, and separated from it, and subdued his inclination. And the Sages said (Berachot 34b): in the place where repentant sinners stand, even the completely righteous cannot stand — meaning: their level is greater than the level of those who never sinned at all, because they subdue their inclination more than they do. And all the prophets commanded regarding teshuvah (Berachot, ibid.), and Israel will be redeemed only through teshuvah (Sanhedrin 97b). And the Torah has already promised that Israel will ultimately do teshuvah at the end of their exile, and will immediately be redeemed, as it is said (Deuteronomy 30:1-3), "and it shall come to pass, when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse which I have set before you, and you shall call them to mind... and you shall return to the Lord your God... then the Lord your God will return your captivity, and have compassion upon you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples..."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:124: Great is teshuvah, for it draws a person near to the Divine Presence, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, Israel, to the Lord your God" (Yoma 86a), and it is said (Amos 4:6), "yet you have not returned to Me, says the Lord." And it is said (Jeremiah 4:1), "if you return, Israel, says the Lord, return to Me" — meaning: if you return in teshuvah, you shall cling to Me. Teshuvah draws the distant near. Last night this person was hated before the Blessed Omnipresent, despised, distant, and abominable, and today he is beloved and cherished, near and dear. And so you find: with the very language by which the Holy One, blessed be He, distances sinners, He draws near those who return, whether individuals or the many, as it is said (Hosea 2:1), "and it shall be, that in the place where it was said to them, 'you are not My people,' it shall be said to them, 'you are the children of the living God.'"
Orchot Tzadikim 26:125: Of Yechonyah, in his wickedness, it is said (Jeremiah 22:30), "write this man childless, a man who shall not prosper in his days..."; "though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet upon My right hand, yet from there I would pluck you off..." (ibid. verse 24). And once he repented in his exile, it is said of his descendant Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:23), "in that day, says the Lord of Hosts, will I take you, O Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, My servant, says the Lord, and will make you as a signet."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:126: How exalted is the virtue of teshuvah! Last night this person was separated from the Lord, God of Israel, blessed be He, as it is said (Isaiah 59:2), "but your iniquities have separated between you and your God"; he cries out and is not answered, as it is said (ibid. 1:15), "even though you multiply prayer, I will not hear"; and he performs commandments and they are flung back in his face, as it is said (ibid. 1:12), "who has required this of your hand, to trample My courts"; "who among you would even shut the doors" (Malachi 1:10); "add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat flesh" (Jeremiah 7:21). But today he is cleaving to the Divine Presence, as it is said (Deuteronomy 4:4), "but you who cling to the Lord your God"; he cries out and is answered at once, as it is said (Isaiah 65:24), "and it shall come to pass, before they call, I will answer"; and he performs commandments and they are accepted with pleasure and joy, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 9:7), "for God has already accepted your works." And not only that, but He desires them, as it is said (Malachi 3:4), "and the offering of Judah and Jerusalem shall be pleasant to the Lord, as in the days of old, and as in former years."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:127: It is the way of repentant sinners to be exceedingly lowly and humble. And if fools revile them for their former deeds, and say to them, "last night you were doing such-and-such," they should not react to it, but hear it and rejoice, knowing this is a merit for them, and that as long as they are ashamed of their past deeds and feel disgraced by them, their merit is increased and their level grows greater. And it is a great sin to say to a repentant sinner, "remember your former deeds," or to mention them before him in order to shame him. And of this it is said (Leviticus 25:17), "and you shall not wrong one another."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:128: Whoever is a repentant sinner should pursue good deeds, and keep far from the schemes of this world, and reflect on the counsel of the Lord and take refuge in His shadow. And should bear the yoke of the Torah of the Lord and the reproach and disgrace of fools, and be like one deaf, blind, and dead, as the matter is said (Psalms 69:8-14), "for I have borne reproach for Your sake... and I made sackcloth my clothing... but as for me, my prayer is to You, O Lord, in a time of favor."
Orchot Tzadikim 27:2: Torah. With three crowns Israel was crowned: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, the crown of kingship (Mishnah Avot 4:13). Aaron merited the crown of priesthood, as it is said, "and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him a covenant of everlasting priesthood" (Numbers 25:13). David, peace upon him, merited the crown of kingship, as it is said, "his seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before Me" (Psalms 89:37). The crown of Torah lies ready and available for all Israel, as it is said, "the Torah Moses commanded us is an inheritance for the congregation of Jacob" (Deuteronomy 33:4) — whoever wishes may come and take it. Perhaps you will say those other crowns are greater than the crown of Torah? Behold it says, "by Me kings reign, and rulers decree justice; by Me princes rule" (Proverbs 8:15-16). From this you learn that the crown of Torah is greater than the crown of priesthood and the crown of kingship (Yoma 72b). And our Sages of blessed memory said (Horayot 13a): an illegitimate child who is a Torah scholar takes precedence over an ignorant High Priest, as it is said, "she is more precious than rubies" (Proverbs 3:15) — more precious than the High Priest who enters the innermost sanctuary.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:3: There is no commandment among all the commandments equal to the study of Torah; rather, the study of Torah is equal to all the commandments, since study leads to practice (Bava Kamma 17a). And what they said, "the study of Torah is equal to all of them" (Mishnah Peah 1:1) — this refers to one who studies with the intent to study and to teach, to keep and to do and to fulfill; and because of his fixed devotion to Torah he cannot fulfill all the commandments, but at a time when he is not studying he does whatever he can, and through this shows his intent to desire the performance of the commandment. And then the study of Torah is equal to all of them, for when he studies about a commandment and desires to fulfill it, he has reward as though he had fulfilled it, since he was delayed only because of his fixed devotion to study, and it follows that the reward for both practice and study is in his hand. But whoever goes idle many times, when he could have performed a commandment during his idleness and does not concern himself with performing it, or who, when he does perform some commandment, is not exact about it as he should be — of him it is not said that "the study of Torah is equal to all of them."
Orchot Tzadikim 27:4: Whoever's heart is set on performing this commandment and fulfilling it properly, and to be crowned with the crown of Torah, should not let his mind wander to idle matters, and should not set his heart on acquiring Torah together with wealth and honor at once. Rather, this is the way of Torah: you shall eat bread with salt, and drink water by measure, and sleep on the ground, and live a life of hardship, and toil in the Torah (Mishnah Avot 6:4).
Orchot Tzadikim 27:5: And if you say: until I gather wealth and until I am free from my business, then I will return and read and study — if this thought arises in your heart, you will never merit the crown of Torah; rather, make your Torah fixed and your work occasional (Mishnah Avot 1:15). And do not say, "when I am free I will study," lest you never become free (Mishnah Avot 2:4).
Orchot Tzadikim 27:6: It is written in the Torah, "it is not in heaven" (Deuteronomy 30:12), meaning: not among the haughty in spirit. "Neither is it beyond the sea" (ibid. verse 13), meaning: not among those who travel overseas (Eruvin 55a). Therefore our Sages of blessed memory said: not everyone who increases in business grows wise (Mishnah Avot 2:5). And our Sages said: minimize business dealings and occupy yourself with Torah (ibid. 4:10).
Orchot Tzadikim 27:7: And because a person occupies himself with Torah for its own sake, and toils and labors for the sake of Heaven, his two kidneys become like two springs, and he brings forth understanding and laws from within himself, things he never learned and things that were not even given to Moses at Sinai. As we find with Abraham our father, of blessed memory, who never learned from any person, but sat and reasoned out the commandments on his own, and learned from his own heart the entire Torah and its commandments, until the verse testified of him, "and he kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws" (Genesis 26:5). And our Sages of blessed memory said that he even knew the laws of eruv tavshilin (see Bereishit Rabbah 95:3). And our Sages of blessed memory further said (Avodah Zarah 14b): Abraham our father, peace upon him, studied four hundred chapters. And who taught him all this? Rather, his two kidneys became like two springs, gushing forth wisdom and Torah for him.
Orchot Tzadikim 27:8: And so we find with Rabbi Eliezer the Great: because he occupied himself so much with Torah, our Sages of blessed memory testified of him that it was revealed to him what was not even revealed to Moses at Sinai (Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer 2). And so our Sages of blessed memory said: from the generation of Moses our teacher, peace upon him, to the generation of Joshua, and from Joshua to the elders, and to the prophets, and to the men of the Great Assembly, and to the Tannaim, and to the Amoraim, and to the Geonim, and to all the sages of every generation who occupied themselves greatly with Torah and gave their souls over to it — the secrets of Torah and the mysteries of wisdom were revealed to them, which a person cannot find on his own.
